pages.title: A double bond changes the possibilities

blocks.text: But-1-ene and but-2-ene share C4H8 but differ in double-bond position. But-2-ene has an additional spatial distinction because its double bond cannot rotate freely. To name, prepare and react with an alkene correctly, first establish exactly which structure is present.

This unit develops alkene naming and isomerism, compares preparation routes and then explains elementary additions. Track the C=C location and the groups on each of its carbons rather than treating every compound with formula CₙH₂ₙ as the same molecule.

pages.transition: A precise alkene name must first locate the double bond.

pages.title: Name the chain that contains the double bond

blocks.text: Choose the appropriate longest parent chain containing C=C and number it to give the double bond the lowest possible locant in these simple examples. Use –ene and write the double bond’s starting position; substituents are then located on that numbered parent.

CH2=C(CH3)CH2CH3 has a four-carbon parent containing C=C. Numbering starts at the terminal CH2, making the double bond position 1 and methyl position 2. The name is 2-methylbut-1-ene. Counting the branch as part of a longer chain that omits the double bond gives an unsuitable parent.

A symmetrical alkene presents equivalent double-bonded environments for the stated addition. An unsymmetrical alkene may give different connectivities depending on which carbon receives each part of the reagent.

pages.transition: The same formula can allow both connectivity and spatial alternatives.

pages.title: Structural and geometrical alternatives

blocks.text: But-1-ene and but-2-ene are position isomers; 2-methylpropene has a different carbon skeleton. All have C4H8. In but-2-ene, each double-bonded carbon has H and CH3, allowing distinct arrangements with the methyl groups on the same or opposite sides.

Cis-but-2-ene has its two methyl groups on the same side; trans-but-2-ene has them on opposite sides. Geometrical isomerism requires two different groups on each carbon of the double bond. Ethene and propene fail that requirement because one double-bonded carbon bears two identical hydrogens.

pages.transition: Selective partial hydrogenation uses that spatial distinction in preparation.

pages.title: Partial hydrogenation: stop at the alkene

blocks.text: An alkyne can take up one H2 to give an alkene, but ordinary active metal catalysts may continue to the alkane. A deactivated palladium catalyst, Lindlar’s catalyst, helps stop at the alkene. Suitable internal alkynes give cis products in this partial hydrogenation.

But-2-yne + H2 with Lindlar’s catalyst gives cis-but-2-ene. Sodium in liquid ammonia instead gives trans-but-2-ene in this example. Ethyne gives ethene, which has no cis/trans pair; do not assign stereochemical labels where the product lacks the required two different groups on each carbon.

pages.transition: Elimination provides another route that creates C=C from a single bond.

pages.title: Remove hydrogen halide to create C=C

blocks.text: Dehydrohalogenation removes H and X from adjacent carbons of an alkyl halide. Heating with alcoholic KOH favours elimination in the elementary preparation scheme. The carbon bearing X is the α carbon; the neighbouring carbon losing H is the β carbon.

CH3CH2Br + KOH(alcoholic, heat) → CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O. Carbon count remains two while a C=C bond forms. The same substrate under aqueous conditions can favour substitution instead; the solvent and conditions should accompany the proposed preparation.

pages.transition: Different removable groups require different elimination-type preparations.

pages.title: Two more ways to remove groups

blocks.text: Vicinal dihalides have halogens on neighbouring carbons. Zinc can remove both: CH2BrCH2Br + Zn → CH2=CH2 + ZnBr2. Alcohol dehydration removes water: CH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O with suitable acid and heating.

Dehalogenation removes two halogen atoms; dehydrohalogenation removes H and X; dehydration removes H and OH as water. Each can create a double bond but begins from a different functional arrangement. Naming the groups removed prevents confusion between the reagents needed.

pages.transition: The newly formed π system explains the characteristic addition reactions.

pages.title: Why the pi bond undergoes addition

blocks.text: The exposed π electron cloud can interact with electrophiles. Addition uses the π bond while creating new σ bonds; the C–C σ framework remains. Physical properties are broadly hydrocarbon-like: low water solubility and increasing boiling points with increasing molecular size.

Hydrogenation: CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3CH3 with a suitable metal catalyst. Halogen addition: CH2=CH2 + Br2 → BrCH2CH2Br in the stated addition conditions. The product is a vicinal dihalide because each original double-bonded carbon receives one bromine.

pages.transition: An unsymmetrical double bond raises an orientation question.

pages.title: Unsymmetrical addition needs a direction rule

blocks.text: For ordinary ionic addition of HX to a simple unsymmetrical alkene, Markovnikov’s rule places H on the double-bonded carbon already bearing more hydrogens, and X mainly on the other carbon. It describes the major product under appropriate conditions, not every possible reaction of an alkene.

Propene, CH3CH=CH2, has one H on the middle carbon and two on the terminal carbon. Ordinary HBr addition therefore gives mainly CH3CHBrCH3, 2-bromopropane. Hydrogen adds to the terminal carbon, while bromine appears at the middle carbon.

pages.transition: Carbocation stability supplies a reason for the Markovnikov product pattern.

pages.title: Explain the rule through the intermediate

blocks.text: Proton addition to propene can form a secondary carbocation at the middle carbon or a primary carbocation at the end. The secondary intermediate is more stable in this simple comparison, so its pathway is favoured. Br⁻ then bonds at the positively charged middle carbon.

The reagent’s negative part does not choose a carbon by counting hydrogens independently of a mechanism. The stability of the intermediate explains the pattern. Radical conditions with peroxides can change HBr addition; specify ordinary ionic conditions when applying the rule here.

For geometrical isomerism, test each C=C carbon independently. In CHCl=CHCl, each has H and Cl, so two relative arrangements are possible. In CH2=CCl2, one carbon has H/H and the other Cl/Cl, so the required distinction fails even though two chlorine atoms are present.

pages.transition: We can now choose structures, preparation routes and addition products consistently.

pages.title: Identify the structure before choosing the route

blocks.text: Locate C=C in the name, distinguish structural from geometrical isomerism and check the two-different-groups condition. Lindlar partial hydrogenation and dissolving-metal reduction can give different spatial products for suitable internal alkynes.

Elimination, dehalogenation and dehydration create C=C from different starting groups. Additions consume π bonding, and Markovnikov orientation for ordinary HX addition follows the favoured carbocation pathway. Conditions and electron reasoning make the product prediction meaningful.

questions.question: Why does propene not show cis/trans isomerism?
questions.answer: Its terminal double-bonded carbon carries two identical H atoms, so the necessary two-different-groups condition fails.

questions.question: Name CH2=C(CH3)CH2CH3.
questions.answer: 2-Methylbut-1-ene: a four-carbon parent containing the double bond, numbered from the C=C end.

questions.question: Which preparation can give cis-but-2-ene from but-2-yne?
questions.answer: Partial hydrogenation with H2 and Lindlar’s catalyst.

questions.question: Distinguish dehalogenation from dehydrohalogenation.
questions.answer: Dehalogenation removes two halogens, commonly from adjacent carbons; dehydrohalogenation removes H and a halogen from adjacent carbons.

questions.question: Why is 2-bromopropane the major ordinary HBr-addition product of propene?
questions.answer: Proton addition that forms the more stable secondary carbocation is favoured, and Br⁻ then attaches at that carbon.

questions.question: Does aqueous KOH always play the same role as alcoholic KOH?
questions.answer: No. Conditions affect reaction pathways; aqueous conditions commonly favour substitution in simple examples, while heated alcoholic base favours elimination.

title: Alkene Isomerism, Preparation and Electrophilic Addition
